chunks.p: NestJS query string filters for Drizzle
chunks.t:
Does parseQuery work with Express 5. 
Yes. It reads Express 5's flat keys such as age[gte] and the nested objects of the qs extended parser, so you do not need to change the query parser setting.

How do I read a query parameter of my own?. 
List it in the ignore option and read it from the query yourself. Any key that is not ignored and not a known parameter is treated as a filter, and an unknown filter column is a 400.

Does the parser cap the page size?. 
No. It only checks that limit is a positive integer. findAll clamps it to pagination.maxLimit, which is 100 by default.

How do I let clients see soft-deleted rows?. 
Pass allowTrash: true to parseQuery. Then withDeleted and onlyDeleted become options; without it they are read as filter columns and rejected.

chunks.p: NestJS query string filters for Drizzle

chunks.t:
Build NestJS Drizzle CRUD endpoints for one table. Define the schema, configure the module, add an empty service and call it from a controller.

To build NestJS Drizzle CRUD endpoints with nestjs-drizzle-crud, you define a Drizzle table,
call DrizzleCrudModule.forRoot once, write an empty service class that extends
SqlBaseCrudService, bind it to the table with forFeature, and call its methods from a
controller. The result is a users API with list, get, create, update and delete routes, plus
filtering, sorting and pagination from the query string.

What you need first. 
Node 20 or later and a PostgreSQL database you can reach through a DATABASE_URL. The steps use
PostgreSQL; for MySQL or SQLite, follow
the matching tab in Installation (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/installation#which-driver-do-i-need) at step 4.

chunks.h: How do I go from an empty project to CRUD endpoints?
chunks.t:
Create a NestJS project. Skip this step if you already have one.

Install the package and the PostgreSQL driver. @nestjs/common, @nestjs/core and reflect-metadata come with the Nest project. See
Install NestJS with Drizzle ORM (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/installation) for the full peer list.

Define the Drizzle table. Create the table in your database with your usual migration tool (drizzle-kit, for example).

The created_at, updated_at and deleted_at keys are not decoration. Soft delete and
timestamps are on by default, and the package looks for columns under exactly those keys in the
table object. Matching them means the service needs no config.

camelCase keys need config. 
With createdAt: timestamp("created_at") the key is createdAt, so name it in forFeature:
config: { softDelete: { column: "deletedAt" }, timestamps: { createdAt: "createdAt", updatedAt: "updatedAt" } }.
A key the table does not have stops the app at startup with a message that names the key to
use. A table with no deleted_at needs softDelete: { enabled: false }. See
Soft delete (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete) and Timestamps (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/timestamps).

chunks.h: How do I go from an empty project to CRUD endpoints?
chunks.t:
Configure the module once. forRoot registers the module globally, so every feature module can use the connection. Because
the module built the connection from connectionString, it also closes it on shutdown. Call
app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts so that happens on SIGTERM too.

chunks.h: Install the package and the PostgreSQL driver
chunks.t:
@nestjs/common, @nestjs/core and reflect-metadata come with the Nest project. See
Install NestJS with Drizzle ORM (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/installation) for the full peer list.

Create the table in your database with your usual migration tool (drizzle-kit, for example).

The created_at, updated_at and deleted_at keys are not decoration. Soft delete and
timestamps are on by default, and the package looks for columns under exactly those keys in the
table object. Matching them means the service needs no config.

camelCase keys need config. 
With createdAt: timestamp("created_at") the key is createdAt, so name it in forFeature:
config: { softDelete: { column: "deletedAt" }, timestamps: { createdAt: "createdAt", updatedAt: "updatedAt" } }.
A key the table does not have stops the app at startup with a message that names the key to
use. A table with no deleted_at needs softDelete: { enabled: false }. See
Soft delete (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete) and Timestamps (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/timestamps).

forRoot registers the module globally, so every feature module can use the connection. Because
the module built the connection from connectionString, it also closes it on shutdown. Call
app.enableShutdownHooks() in main.ts so that happens on SIGTERM too.

The four type parameters are the row type, the create DTO, the update DTO and the filter type.
All four are required. CrudFilter accepts every filter the package understands.

Keep the service empty. 
No @Injectable(), no constructor, no injected db. forFeature builds the service and hands
it its config, so a constructor parameter or a provider entry breaks registration. Override the
protected hooks (validateCreate, beforeCreate and so on) when you need custom logic.

chunks.h: Bind the service to its table
chunks.t:
forFeature provides and exports UsersService. Do not also list it under providers: Nest
would then build its own copy with no config.

chunks.h: Call the service from a controller
chunks.t:
Import the DTOs as values, not with import type: Nest reads the runtime class through decorator
metadata. find returns null for a missing row, so the controller turns that into a 404 itself.
update and softDelete throw a 404 on their own.

ParseIntPipe fits because id is a serial column. For a uuid key use ParseUUIDPipe; see
Primary keys (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/primary-keys).

The list route answers with the findAll envelope:

A second POST with the same email is a 409, because the unique violation becomes a
DuplicateEntityException. After the DELETE, the row is soft deleted: it disappears from the
list and from GET /users/1, and restore(1) would bring it back.

c.s:
curl -X POST localhost:3000/users -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"}'
curl -g 'localhost:3000/users?name[iContains]=ali&sortBy=-created_at'
curl -X PATCH localhost:3000/users/1 -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Alicia"}'
curl -X DELETE localhost:3000/users/1

chunks.t:
UsersService inherits every method in CRUD operations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/crud-operations), typed against
User. The ones this controller did not use yet:

Method What it does 
--- --- 
findOne(where) First row matching an equality object, such as { email } 
count(filters) / exists(id) Count matching rows, or check one id 
findByCursor(filters, pagination) Keyset pagination with an opaque nextCursor 
restore(id) / forceDelete(id) Bring a soft deleted row back, or remove it for good 
delete(id) Hard delete of a live row 
upsert(dto, upsert) Insert, or update on a unique key conflict 
massCreate, massUpdate, massSoftDelete, massRestore, massDelete One transaction for a list of rows or ids 

To skip the controller entirely, the controller factory (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/controller-factory) generates
these routes, bulk and trash routes included.

Why does my app fail at startup with softDelete.column is deleted_at?. 
Soft delete is on by default and the table has no column under the key deleted_at. Name your key with softDelete: { column: "deletedAt" } in forFeature, or turn it off with softDelete: { enabled: false }.

Do I need @Injectable() on the service?. 
No. DrizzleCrudModule.forFeature creates the service with a factory and passes its config to the constructor. Adding a constructor parameter or a providers entry for it breaks that.

Does DELETE remove the row?. 
In this controller it calls softDelete, which sets deleted_at and hides the row from reads. Call delete for a hard delete of a live row, or forceDelete to remove a row whether it is soft deleted or not.

Which query parameters does the list route accept?. 
Everything parseQuery reads: column filters such as name[iContains]=ali, sortBy, page, limit, fields, with and more. Unknown columns are a 400.

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.t:
Drizzle filter by relation in NestJS: paths at any depth and some, none, every on collections, compiled to EXISTS subqueries that never multiply rows.

To filter by relation with Drizzle in this package, use the relation name as a filter key: { state: { country: { code: "IN" } } } follows a path through relations to any depth, and { states: { none: { name: "Kerala" } } } quantifies a collection with some, none or every. Only the top-level belongs-to is joined. Everything else compiles to an IN, EXISTS or NOT EXISTS subquery, so parent rows are never multiplied and total stays right.

Declare the relations first. 
A relation filter only works on relations declared in the entity's relations config, and a
collection needs type: "hasMany" or type: "manyToMany". Without a type the relation is a
belongs-to. Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations) covers the config; Filtering with Drizzle in
NestJS (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/filtering) covers the column operators used inside a relation filter.

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: How do I filter through more than one relation?
chunks.t:
Nest the relation names, as declared in each relation's own relations config. A belongs-to chain from cities to countries looks like this:

The top-level belongs-to (state) is joined with a LEFT JOIN. Each deeper level is a correlated EXISTS on its own table alias:

Because each subquery gets its own alias, a relation back to a table already in the query (a self relation) still resolves. With soft delete on, a soft-deleted related row never matches, at any level.

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: How do I use some, none and every?
chunks.t:
On a has-many or many-to-many relation, the value is either a filter (meaning some) or an object whose keys are all quantifiers:

Filter Keeps parents that SQL 
--- --- --- 
{ states: { name: "Kerala" } } have at least one matching row id IN (SELECT...) 
{ states: { some: { name: "Kerala" } } } the same id IN (SELECT...) 
{ states: { some: {} } } have any row at all id IN (SELECT...) 
{ states: { none: { name: "Kerala" } } } have no matching row NOT EXISTS (...) 
{ states: { none: {} } } have no rows at all NOT EXISTS (...) 
{ states: { every: { name: { startsWith: "Ba" } } } } have no row that fails the filter NOT EXISTS (... AND NOT coalesce(filter, false)) 

Rules worth knowing:

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: How do I use some, none and every?
chunks.t:
- Several quantifiers in one object are ANDed: { states: { some: { name: "Kerala" }, none: { code: "XX" } } }.
- An empty plain filter, { states: {} }, adds nothing. Write { states: { some: {} } } to mean "has at least one".
- The object counts as quantifiers only when every key is some, none or every and the related table has no column by that name. Mixing a quantifier with a column ({ some: {...}, name: "x" }) is read as a plain filter, so some is an unknown column and the call is a 400.
- A quantifier value must be an object of column filters, otherwise 400.

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: What does every mean for a parent with no rows?
chunks.t:
It matches. every means "no related row fails the filter", which is true when there are none, as in Prisma. Add some: {} when you need at least one:

A related row whose filter evaluates to NULL (a NULL column, say) counts as failing, which is what the coalesce(..., false) is for. Soft-deleted related rows are ignored by all three quantifiers. An every with an empty filter adds nothing.

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: Do relation filters work in groups and counts?
chunks.t: Yes. A relation filter, at any depth and with any quantifier, can sit inside and, or and not, and findAll, findByCursor, count and countBy all build their WHERE with the same compiler:

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: How do I send relation filters in a query string?
chunks.t:
Use brackets or dots, the same as for one level. parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing) builds the filter object for you:

states[some]= with no column means "has at least one".

c.s:
GET /cities?state[country][code]=IN
GET /cities?state.country.code=IN
GET /countries?states[none][name]=Kerala
GET /countries?states[every][name][startsWith]=Ba
GET /countries?states[some]=

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.h: How do allowlists treat a relation path?
chunks.t: filterableColumns names the full dotted path to the column. "state.country.code" allows the city filter above and nothing else on country. Quantifiers do not appear in the path, so "states.name" allows states[none][name] as well as states[name]. See allowlists (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists).

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM
chunks.t:
Does filtering by a has-many relation duplicate rows?. 
No. A has-many or many-to-many filter compiles to IN (SELECT...) or NOT EXISTS (...), never a join, so each parent appears once and total and pagination stay correct.

Which relations are joined?. 
Only a belongs-to at the top level of the filter, with a LEFT JOIN. A belongs-to deeper in a path is an EXISTS subquery, and a collection is always a subquery.

Does every match a parent with no related rows?. 
Yes, as in Prisma. Combine it with some: {} when the parent must have at least one related row.

Are soft-deleted related rows considered?. 
No. With soft delete on for the related table, a soft-deleted row never matches a relation filter, and some, none and every all ignore it.

chunks.p: Filter by relation in Drizzle ORM

chunks.t:
Declare Drizzle relations in NestJS and eager-load belongs-to, has-many, many-to-many and nested relations without N+1 queries.

Drizzle relations in NestJS are declared in the entity's forFeature config under relations, keyed by relation name, and loaded with options.relations on any read or write. Three shapes are supported, and each can nest: belongs-to (an object or null), has-many and many-to-many (arrays). No shape ever runs a query per row, so eager loading a page of 50 rows costs the same number of queries as a page of 5.

Only a top-level belongs-to is joined. 
A belongs-to declared on the service's own table rides along in the main query as a LEFT JOIN.
Everything else (has-many, many-to-many, and every nested level whatever its shape) is loaded by
one batched IN (...) query per relation. A collection is never joined, because a join would
multiply parent rows and break total and pagination.

These relations are config objects that point at Drizzle tables. The package does not read Drizzle's
own relations() helper, so you can keep or drop that for the Drizzle query API as you like.

chunks.h: How do I avoid N+1 queries?
chunks.t:
Ask for the relation instead of looping. find, findOne, findAll and findByCursor accept
options.relations, and the service batches the loads:

Fetching the countries and then querying states inside a loop is 1 + N queries. That is the pattern
this replaces.

Relation SQL Extra queries Result 
--- --- --- --- 
top-level belongsTo (default) LEFT JOIN in the main query 0 object, or null when unmatched 
hasMany SELECT... WHERE fk IN (parent keys) 1 per relation, for the whole page array, [] when empty 
manyToMany SELECT... FROM join JOIN target... WHERE fk IN (parent keys) 1 per relation, for the whole page array, [] when empty 
nested (any shape, including belongs-to) batched IN (...) against the level above 1 per relation per level as above 

Sibling relations load concurrently, so three collections are three parallel queries, not three
round trips in sequence.

chunks.h: How do I avoid N+1 queries?
chunks.t:
A level with more parent keys than one statement can bind is split, since 3.8.0: the keys go out in
chunks of 64,535 on PostgreSQL and MySQL (31,766 on SQLite, 90 on Cloudflare D1), so a nested load
whose level holds 70,000 keys is two queries for that relation instead of a 400. All the children of
one parent come from the same chunk, so grouping and orderBy are unchanged. Override the protected
relationChunkSize(db) to load in smaller pieces.

chunks.h: How do I declare a belongs-to relation?
chunks.t:
Name the foreign-key column on this table with localKey. A belongs-to is a many-to-one or
one-to-one link, and it is the default type.

The key of the entry (state here) is the relation name. You use it in options.relations, in
filters, in select paths and as the property on the returned row.

chunks.h: How do I declare a has-many relation?
chunks.t:
Set type: 'hasMany' and name the column on the child table that points back here with foreignKey:

When the service is built, it checks that each relation has its table and the settings its shape
requires (localKey, foreignKey, or the three through settings), including nested relations,
and throws with the relation's path if one is missing. It does not check that the named columns
exist, so a misspelled column name leaves the relation out of the result instead of failing.

chunks.h: How do I declare a many-to-many relation?
chunks.t:
Name the join table and its two foreign-key columns:

The join table never appears in the result. Its key travels with each row long enough to group it
onto the right parent, and is then removed.

Nested collections key on their own table. 
Before 3.3.1 a nested collection borrowed the root service's primaryKey. With a root keyed on
uid, comment.author.posts looked for author.uid and came back empty. A nested level now uses
the primary key column of the table it hangs off (authors.id here), so parentKey is only needed
when the join column is something else.

chunks.h: How do I eager-load a relation of a relation?
chunks.t:
Give the relation its own relations map, then address it with a dotted path in options.relations:

Each level is one batched query for every row at that level, so 50 countries with 200 states and 900
cities is still 4 queries. Nesting works for every shape, including a belongs-to chain:

Asking for state.country pulls in state on its own, so you do not have to list both. A name that
is not configured is dropped, along with the rest of its path.

chunks.h: How do I order a collection?
chunks.t:
Set orderBy on the relation, and the children come back sorted by SQL rather than in insertion
order:

An orderBy entry that names a column the target table does not have is warned about and skipped,
the same way defaultSort behaves.

chunks.h: What does an eager-loaded row look like?
chunks.t:
The relation appears as a property named after it:

An unmatched belongs-to comes back as null, never as an object full of nulls. A parent with no
children gets [], so callers can iterate without a guard.

Soft delete applies to related tables too. When soft delete is on for the service and a related
table has a column under the same key, its deleted rows are hidden: a deleted parent loads as null
and deleted children are left out of the collection. See Soft delete in Drizzle ORM (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/soft-delete).

chunks.h: Why is a collection not joined?
chunks.t:
Because a join would break the page. One country with four states becomes four rows, count( )
returns 4 instead of 1, and limit 50 cuts a country in half. The batched IN (...) query keeps one
row per parent and keeps total honest. This holds for has-many and many-to-many alike.

The count query follows the same rule. findAll joins the eager-loaded belongs-to relations and the
relations your filters use into the data query, but only the filter relations into the count query,
so eager loading never changes total.

chunks.h: How do I filter by a related column?
chunks.t:
Use the relation name as a filter key, with a nested object of the related table's columns:

A filter on a collection compiles to a subquery, never a join, for the same reason a collection is
never joined:

That reads as "parents with at least one matching child". Collection filters accept the same
operators as any other filter, and the predicate applies to the count query too.

chunks.h: How do I filter across more than one level?
chunks.t:
Often you can filter on the intermediate table's columns, so you do not need a relation to the far
table:

Or filter through the relation chain itself, { state: { country: { code: 'IN' } } }. Below the
first belongs-to, each level is an EXISTS subquery on an aliased table rather than a join. Use
some, none and every to quantify collections. See Relation filters (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relation-filters)
for the full syntax.

c.s:
// cities -> states (direct relation) -> countries (via states.country_id)
await citiesService.findAll({ state: { country_id: 3 } });

chunks.h: How do I select relation columns?
chunks.t:
options.select takes dotted paths, so you can narrow a relation instead of loading every column:

The child keeps its foreign key even when you do not list it, because that column maps each child
back to its parent. The parent likewise keeps any key a nested level needs. See
column selection (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/column-selection) for the full rules.

chunks.h: Can clients request relations over HTTP?
chunks.t:
Yes. parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing) turns?with=region,states into options.relations and?region[name]=Asia into a relation filter. Limit what a client may load with the
loadableRelations allowlist (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists); listing states.cities also allows states.

- A top-level belongs-to is always a LEFT join. To drop rows with no match, filter on the
relation: { state: { id: { isNotNull: true } } }.
- A collection is not paginated per parent. orderBy sorts the children, but every matching
child is returned. Write a custom method for "the latest three per parent".
- Join-table columns are not returned. If the join table carries data of its own (a role, a
position), model it as an entity with two belongs-to relations.

chunks.h: Can I load relations on a write, or count them?
chunks.t:
Yes. create, update, restore, upsert and the mass writes take options.relations and return
the rows with them loaded, using the same batched loaders, and a create body can write children too.
See Relations on writes (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations-on-writes). options.counts adds a _count object for
collections, one grouped query per relation; see Aggregates (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates).

Does eager loading cause N+1 queries?. 
No. A top-level belongs-to is joined into the main query, and every other relation costs one batched query per relation per level for the whole result, whatever the row count.

Which relation types are supported?. 
Belongs-to (the default), has-many and many-to-many through a join table. Any of them can nest with a dotted path such as states.cities.

Why are has-many relations not loaded with a JOIN?. 
A join returns one row per child, which inflates total and breaks limit. A batched IN (...) query keeps one row per parent.

Does the package use Drizzle. 
No. Relations are declared in the forFeature config and point at Drizzle tables directly.

What does an unmatched belongs-to relation return?. 
null, never an object of nulls. An empty has-many or many-to-many relation returns [].

Drizzle nested create in NestJS. Write a row and its related rows in one transaction, return writes with relations, and attach or sync links.

Drizzle nested create in NestJS works through writableRelations: list a relation there, put the related rows in the create body under the relation's name, and the package writes the parent and its children in one transaction. Every write method also takes options.relations and returns its rows with those relations loaded, and attach, detach and sync change many-to-many links with set-based statements.

Define the relations first. 
Every example here uses relations declared in forFeature config. If you have not set those up, start with Relations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/relations). Nested create needs RETURNING, so it runs on PostgreSQL only.

chunks.h: How do I get a created row back with its relations?
chunks.t:
Pass relations (and counts, see Aggregates (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/aggregates)) as you would on find:

That is one INSERT plus one query per relation. A mass write loads the relations of every row it wrote in one query per relation too, so massCreate of 10 posts with relations: ['author'] is an INSERT and one SELECT, not ten. Since 3.8.0 a mass write that opened its own transaction loads them after it commits, so its row locks are held for less time; inside your transaction, or with a counts filter (whose value could fail and must roll the write back), they load inside it as before. massCreate always loads inside its transaction since 3.8.1, so a failed load stores nothing (see bulk operations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/bulk-operations#do-bulk-writes-work-with-relations-scope-and-versions)).

These methods load relations onto what they return:

Method Loads relations and counts 
--- --- 
create, massCreate yes 
update, massUpdate yes 
upsert, massUpsert yes 
restore, massRestore yes 
attach, detach, sync yes, plus the relation they changed

chunks.h: How do I get a created row back with its relations?
chunks.t: The relation paths are checked against loadableRelations (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) before anything is written, so a bad path is a 400 and leaves the table untouched.

chunks.h: How do I create a row with its children in one call?
chunks.t:
Allow the relation, then send the children in the body.

Declare the relation and allow writing it. List the relation in writableRelations next to its definition:

Put the children in the body under the relation's name. The author and both posts are written in one transaction: one INSERT for the author and one multi-row INSERT for the posts, with author_id set for you.

Handle a failing child. If a child fails, the parent is rolled back too, and the call answers with the child's error: a bad enum value is a 400, a duplicate key a 409. If you passed your own transaction, the nested writes join it instead of opening a new one.

chunks.h: Declare the relation and allow writing it
chunks.t: List the relation in writableRelations next to its definition:

chunks.h: Put the children in the body under the relation's name
chunks.t: The author and both posts are written in one transaction: one INSERT for the author and one multi-row INSERT for the posts, with author_id set for you.

If a child fails, the parent is rolled back too, and the call answers with the child's error: a bad enum value is a 400, a duplicate key a 409. If you passed your own transaction, the nested writes join it instead of opening a new one.

chunks.h: What shapes does a nested body take?
chunks.t:
The body value depends on the relation type:

Relation Body value What happens 
--- --- --- 
has-many an array of objects One multi-row INSERT, with the foreign key set to the new row's key. 
belongs-to an object The related row is inserted first and its key goes on the new row (localKey). 
many-to-many an array of ids, objects, or both Objects are inserted into the related table in one statement, then every id is linked through the join table. 

A few rules apply to every shape:

chunks.h: What shapes does a nested body take?
chunks.t:
- Nested writes run on create only, and go one level deep.
- Only the related table's own columns are written, never its soft delete column. Other keys in a child object are dropped.
- The timestamps and the tenant scope (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy) are set on a child row when the related table has those columns.
- On a scoped entity, a child's belongs-to key that the nested relation declares in its own relations must point at a row of the caller's tenant, or the create is a 400 and nothing is written. An undeclared child key is left to the database's foreign key.
- A relation key set to null is skipped.
- A wrong shape (an object for has-many, an array for belongs-to) is a 400.
- On MySQL, which has no RETURNING, a nested create is a 400.
- On SQLite it works with a driver that has async transactions, such as libSQL. On Cloudflare D1 and synchronous drivers it throws a TransactionException.

chunks.h: What if writableRelations is not set?
chunks.t: Then nested writes are off. A relation key in the body is left alone and Drizzle ignores it, which is how 3.4 behaved. With the list set, a relation key that is not in it is a 400, the same way writableColumns (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/allowlists) treats a column. A trusted server-side call can pass skipAllowlists: true to write any declared relation.

chunks.h: How do I attach or detach many-to-many rows?
chunks.t:
Call attach, detach or sync with the row's id, the relation name and the related ids:

Method Signature What it does 
--- --- --- 
attach attach(id, relation, relatedIds, options?) Adds links. Ids already linked are skipped. 
detach detach(id, relation, relatedIds?, options?) Removes the given links, or every link when relatedIds is left out. 
sync sync(id, relation, relatedIds, options?) Adds the missing links and removes the rest, so the links match relatedIds exactly. [] removes every link. 

Each method returns Promise: the row with that relation loaded, plus anything in options.relations. Each runs in one transaction and is set based whatever the number of ids: one SELECT reads the row, one checks the targets exist, one finds the links already there, one INSERT adds the rest (sync adds one DELETE), and one query per relation loads the result onto the row read first. A nested create skips the "already linked" SELECT, since a row created in the same call has no links yet. Duplicates in the list are ignored. The related rows themselves are never changed or deleted.

With global hooks on, they raise attach, detach and sync events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events).

c.s:
await posts.attach(2, 'tags', [1, 2]);         // link tags 1 and 2
await posts.detach(2, 'tags', [1]);            // unlink tag 1
await posts.detach(2, 'tags');                 // unlink every tag
const post = await posts.sync(2, 'tags', [2]); // links are exactly [2] now
post.tags; // [{ id: 2, name: 'tech' }]

chunks.h: What errors can attach, detach and sync return?
chunks.t:
Cause Result 
--- --- 
The row does not exist, or is outside the caller's scope (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/multi-tenancy) 404 
A target id that does not exist or is soft-deleted 400 BulkOperationException with one 404 entry per missing id 
A target of another tenant, when the related table has the scope column Counted as missing: a 404 entry 
The relation is not a many-to-many 400 
writableRelations is set and does not list the relation 400 
relatedIds is not an array of plain ids 400 

When writableRelations is unset, attach, detach and sync work on any many-to-many relation.

Can I create a row and its children in one call?. 
Yes. List the relation in writableRelations and send the children under the relation's name in the create body. The parent and children are written in one transaction.

Does nested create work on update?. 
No. Nested writes run on create only. To change many-to-many links on an existing row, use attach, detach or sync.

Does nested create work on MySQL?. 
No. It needs RETURNING to know the new keys, so on MySQL a nested create is a 400.

Does sync delete the related rows?. 
No. sync only adds and removes rows in the join table. The related rows themselves are never changed or deleted.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.h: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.t:
Drizzle SELECT FOR UPDATE in NestJS. Pass lock or forNoKeyUpdate to find, findOne or findAll inside a transaction to lock rows on PostgreSQL or MySQL.

For a Drizzle SELECT... FOR UPDATE in NestJS, pass lock: 'update' (or 'share', or forNoKeyUpdate: true) to find, findOne, findAll or findByCursor, together with a transaction. The package adds Drizzle's.for(...) clause to the query, naming only the service's own table, and the rows stay locked until the transaction commits or rolls back. Row locks work on PostgreSQL and MySQL; on SQLite asking for one is a 400.

A lock without a transaction does nothing useful. 
Pass { transaction: tx } with the lock. Without it the SELECT runs in its own implicit transaction, and the lock is released the moment the statement ends, before your write.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.h: How do I lock a row before updating it?
chunks.t:
Read it with lock: 'update' inside a transaction, then write in the same transaction:

A second transaction that runs the same find waits until the first one ends, so it reads the new balance instead of a stale one. That is the lost update this prevents. See Transactions (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/transactions) for executeSqlTransaction and db.transaction.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.t:
Two fields on SqlOperationOptions. The SQL below is PostgreSQL's; MySQL differs as described further down:

Option SQL Blocks 
--- --- --- 
lock: 'update' FOR UPDATE OF <table Every other lock and every write to the rows. 
forNoKeyUpdate: true FOR NO KEY UPDATE OF <table Other writes, but not foreign key checks. 
lock: 'share' FOR SHARE OF <table Writes, but not other FOR SHARE readers. 
lock: 'none' or unset none Nothing.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.h: When should I use FOR NO KEY UPDATE?
chunks.t: Use it when you lock a parent row but other transactions may still insert child rows that reference it. FOR NO KEY UPDATE is like FOR UPDATE, but it does not conflict with the key-share lock PostgreSQL takes when it checks a foreign key, so inserting a child row (an audit log entry, say) does not wait for your transaction.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.h: Which read methods accept a lock?
chunks.t:
find, findOne, findAll and findByCursor:

On findAll and findByCursor the lock goes on the data query only. The COUNT( ) query is not locked. The write methods (create, update, delete, softDelete, restore) do not take a lock option: lock with a find first, in the same transaction, as above.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.h: Can I lock a row and eager-load a belongs-to relation?
chunks.t:
Yes. The lock always names the base table (FOR UPDATE OF <table ), so only the service's own rows are locked and the LEFT JOINed relation is not:

Before 3.3.1 the lock covered every table in the query, and PostgreSQL refused it with FOR UPDATE cannot be applied to the nullable side of an outer join.

c.s:
const post = await this.find(id, { lock: 'update', relations: ['author'], transaction: tx });
// SELECT ... FROM posts LEFT JOIN users ... FOR UPDATE OF "posts"

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.h: Do row locks work on MySQL and SQLite?
chunks.t:
On MySQL, yes, since 3.7.0. lock: 'update' adds FOR UPDATE and lock: 'share' adds FOR SHARE. MySQL has no FOR NO KEY UPDATE, so forNoKeyUpdate: true becomes FOR UPDATE, the stronger lock. MySQL has no OF <table form in Drizzle, so with an eager belongs-to the joined parent row is locked too. Before 3.7.0 the options were accepted and ignored on MySQL.

On SQLite, no. SQLite locks the whole database for a write and has no row locks, so lock (other than "none") or forNoKeyUpdate is a 400 rather than a lock that is silently not there.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.h: Can I use SKIP LOCKED or NOWAIT?
chunks.t: Not through the package options: lock and forNoKeyUpdate only choose the lock strength. For a job queue that needs SKIP LOCKED, use Drizzle's own.for('update', { skipLocked: true }) on tx inside the same transaction, and pass the same tx to the package calls that follow.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE
chunks.t:
Does lock work without a transaction?. 
The clause is added, but the lock ends with the statement because there is no surrounding transaction. Always pass { transaction: tx } with a lock.

Which tables does the lock cover?. 
On PostgreSQL, only the service's own table: the package adds OF <table, so joined belongs-to relations are not locked. On MySQL the joined rows are locked too.

What happens if I set both lock and forNoKeyUpdate?. 
forNoKeyUpdate wins and the query uses FOR NO KEY UPDATE.

Should I use a row lock or optimistic locking?. 
Use a row lock when one transaction reads and writes a row in one go and others should wait. Use optimistic locking with a version column for a read, edit, save flow where the edit happens in a client.

chunks.p: Row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE

chunks.t:
Soft delete rows in NestJS with Drizzle ORM. A deleted_at column hides them from reads, restore brings them back and forceDelete purges.

Soft delete in Drizzle ORM, with this package, means softDelete(id) sets a deleted_at timestamp on the row instead of removing it. Every read then adds deleted_at IS NULL, so the row disappears from find, findAll, count and the rest. restore(id) clears the column and brings the row back, and forceDelete(id) removes it for good. Soft delete is on by default for every entity.

The setting names the key, not the SQL column. 
softDelete.column is the key in your Drizzle table object, deleted_at by default. A camelCase
schema such as deletedAt: timestamp('deleted_at') needs column: 'deletedAt'. Since 3.3.1 a
wrong key stops the service at startup with a message that names the right one, for example:
softDelete.column is "deleted_at", but the table has no column under that key. The column
"deleted_at" is declared under the key "deletedAt"; set softDelete.column to "deletedAt".
Before 3.3.1 the same mistake made every read fail with a 500.

chunks.h: How do I enable soft delete?
chunks.t:
Add a nullable timestamp column. The column must accept null. The package writes new Date() to it on softDelete and null on
restore.

Keep the project default, or set it per entity. Soft delete is already on in forRoot. Set defaults.softDelete: false to turn it off for the whole
project:

Per entity, forFeature can turn it off or point it at another column:

The entity config merges with the project default one level deep, so
{ softDelete: { column: 'archived_at' } } keeps enabled from the project setting.

Delete, list and restore. A table without the column. 
If a table has no soft delete column, set config: { softDelete: { enabled: false } } for that
entity (or defaults: { softDelete: false } for the project). Otherwise the service refuses to
start and names the missing key.

The column must accept null. The package writes new Date() to it on softDelete and null on
restore.

chunks.h: Keep the project default, or set it per entity
chunks.t:
Soft delete is already on in forRoot. Set defaults.softDelete: false to turn it off for the whole
project:

Per entity, forFeature can turn it off or point it at another column:

The entity config merges with the project default one level deep, so
{ softDelete: { column: 'archived_at' } } keeps enabled from the project setting.

A table without the column. 
If a table has no soft delete column, set config: { softDelete: { enabled: false } } for that
entity (or defaults: { softDelete: false } for the project). Otherwise the service refuses to
start and names the missing key.

c.s:
await usersService.softDelete(42);                              // hidden from reads
await usersService.findAll({}, {}, { onlyDeleted: true });      // the trash
await usersService.restore(42);                                 // back in reads
await usersService.forceDelete(42);                             // gone for good

chunks.h: What do the soft delete methods return?
chunks.t:
Method Returns When it fails 
--- --- --- 
softDelete(id, options?) Promise<boolean, true when the row was marked EntityNotFoundException (404) when the row does not exist or is already in the trash 
restore(id, options?) Promise, the restored row EntityNotFoundException (404) when no row has that id 
massSoftDelete(ids, options?) Promise<boolean BulkOperationException listing the ids that are missing or already in the trash; nothing changes 
massRestore(ids, options?) Promise, in the order of ids BulkOperationException listing the ids that do not exist; nothing changes 
forceDelete(id, options?) Promise<boolean EntityNotFoundException (404) when no row has that id 
massForceDelete(ids, options?) Promise<boolean BulkOperationException listing the ids that do not exist 

The mass methods run in a transaction: one SELECT checks the ids exist, then one
UPDATE... WHERE id IN (...) (or DELETE) writes them all. Calling any soft delete or restore
method on an entity with soft delete turned off is a 400 BadRequestException.

chunks.h: What do the soft delete methods return?
chunks.t:
restore only takes a row from the trash. 
restore on a live row is a 404, before any hook or event runs. To ask whether a row is in the
trash, use usersService.exists(42, { onlyDeleted: true }).

All of them. find, findOne, findAll, findByCursor, count, countBy, exists and
fullTextSearch add deleted_at IS NULL to their WHERE.

Related tables follow the same rule when they have a column under the same key. A soft-deleted
belongs-to parent comes back as null on an eager load, deleted children are left out of a has-many
or many-to-many collection, and a relation filter such as { author: { name: 'Bob' } } does not
match a deleted author.

A filter on the column itself, such as { deleted_at: { isNotNull: true } }, still returns nothing,
because the default deleted_at IS NULL is ANDed with it. Use the flags below instead.

chunks.h: How do I list soft-deleted rows?
chunks.t:
Pass onlyDeleted: true for the trash, or withDeleted: true for live and deleted rows together.
Both work on every read listed above.

The flags only change the service's own table. Related tables keep hiding their deleted rows, so an
eager-loaded parent that is in the trash is still null. onlyDeleted on an entity without soft
delete is a 400.

Over HTTP, parseQuery (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/query-parsing) reads?onlyDeleted=true and?withDeleted=true
only when you opt in with allowTrash: true. Without it they are unknown filter columns, so a client
cannot open the trash on a route that is not meant to show it.

chunks.h: How do I purge a soft-deleted row?
chunks.t:
Call forceDelete(id). It hard-deletes the row whether it is in the trash or not, and runs the
delete hooks. massForceDelete(ids) does the same for a set of ids in one statement.

delete(id) only sees live rows, so it answers 404 for a row that is already in the trash, and so
does massDelete. Because delete takes the same read options, delete(id, { withDeleted: true })
is the long way of writing forceDelete(id).

c.s:
await usersService.forceDelete(42);           // gone, even if it was soft-deleted
await usersService.massForceDelete([7, 8, 9]); // one DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...)

chunks.t:
Method Behaviour 
--- --- 
softDelete(id, options?) Sets deleted_at to now. Reads exclude the row afterwards. 
massSoftDelete(ids, options?) Soft delete of a set, one statement, in a transaction. 
delete(id, options?) Removes the row. Answers 404 for a row already in the trash. 
massDelete(ids, options?) Removes live rows, one statement, in a transaction. 
forceDelete(id, options?) Removes the row whether it is in the trash or not. 
massForceDelete(ids, options?) Removes live and trashed rows, one statement, in a transaction. 

Use softDelete when you want the action to be reversible or auditable. Use delete or
forceDelete when the row has to be gone, for example a right-to-erasure request.

chunks.h: What else changes when a row is soft-deleted?
chunks.t:
- updated_at moves. With timestamps (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/timestamps) on, softDelete and restore set
updated_at to now as well.
- The version moves. With optimistic locking (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/optimistic-locking), both bump the version
column, and both accept expectedVersion.
- Bodies cannot touch the column. A create or update body that sets deleted_at has the key
dropped, so a client cannot hide or resurrect a row by accident. Name the column in
writableColumns if you really want it writable.
- Hooks and events fire. beforeSoftDelete / afterSoftDelete and beforeRestore /
afterRestore run around the write. With hooks.enableGlobalHooks on, the module also raises
softDelete and restore events (https://crud.avytrix.dev/docs/events).

Is soft delete on by default?. 
Yes. Every entity uses a deleted_at key unless you set defaults.softDelete: false in forRoot or softDelete: { enabled: false } for the entity.

What does softDelete return when the row does not exist?. 
It throws EntityNotFoundException, which Nest returns as a 404. The same happens when the row is already in the trash.

How do I show soft-deleted rows?. 
Pass onlyDeleted: true for the trash or withDeleted: true for everything. Over HTTP, parseQuery accepts them only with allowTrash: true.

How do I permanently delete a soft-deleted row?. 
Call forceDelete(id), or massForceDelete(ids) for a set. Plain delete answers 404 for a row that is already in the trash.

Does soft delete hide related rows too?. 
Yes, when the related table has a column under the same key. A deleted parent loads as null and deleted children are left out of collections.

Use NestJS with Drizzle on SQLite, libSQL (Turso) or Cloudflare D1. What works, what is a 400, and why D1 cannot run bulk writes or nested creates.

Since 3.7.0 the package runs on SQLite with dialect: "sqlite". You build the Drizzle instance with your SQLite driver and pass it as db; the module does not open SQLite connections itself. Reads, writes, filters, relations, upsert and keyset pages work as on PostgreSQL, with RETURNING. Full-text search, row locks and the PostgreSQL-only operators are a 400. Bulk writes need a driver with async transactions, such as libSQL.

Bulk writes need an async transaction. 
Mass writes, nested creates and attach / detach / sync run in an interactive transaction
with savepoints. libSQL (@libsql/client) has one. Cloudflare D1 has none, and synchronous
drivers (better-sqlite3, bun:sqlite, sql.js) cannot wait for async work inside theirs. On those,
the calls throw a TransactionException (500) that names the reason instead of half working.
The single-row methods are not affected.

chunks.h: How do I connect to SQLite or libSQL?
chunks.t:
Install @libsql/client, build the Drizzle instance and pass it as db:

A db you pass in is yours to close. connectionString is not accepted for "sqlite": it is a startup error that tells you to pass db.

chunks.h: How should I declare the SQLite tables?
chunks.t:
Use sqliteTable from drizzle-orm/sqlite-core. Two details matter to the service:

- Timestamps and soft delete need date columns. The service writes a JavaScript Date into created_at, updated_at and deleted_at, so declare them as integer('created_at', { mode: 'timestamp_ms' }) (or mode: 'timestamp'). A plain text column does not take a Date.
- Foreign keys must be on. SQLite only enforces references with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON. libSQL turns it on for its local databases; with another driver, run the pragma when you open the connection. Without it, a missing parent is not an error at all, so there is no 400 or 409 to map.

chunks.h: What works on SQLite, and what is a 400?
chunks.t:
Feature On SQLite 
--- --- 
find, findAll, count, countBy, findByCursor Yes. Keyset pages follow SQLite's NULL order (first ascending, last descending) 
Filters, relation filters, sort, select, relations, counts Yes 
Writes read back with RETURNING Yes, sql.useReturning defaults to true 
search in ilike mode, ilike, iContains and friends LIKE... ESCAPE '\', so %, _ and \ in the term match literally 
contains, startsWith, endsWith with sql.caseSensitive: true Case-sensitive since 3.7.2: they compile to GLOB, with,? and [ in the value matched literally 
like Plain LIKE, which ignores ASCII case on SQLite whatever sql.caseSensitive says 
Bound parameters per statement 32,766 (libSQL and SQLite's default SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER), 100 on D1. Past it is a 400 before the statement runs 
upsert, massUpsert ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, including the tenant scope guard 
Nested creates, bulk writes, attach / detach / sync Yes on libSQL; TransactionException on D1 and synchronous drivers 
Optimistic locking, tenant scope, soft delete, events Yes 
fullTextSearch, search.mode: "fullText" 400 
lock, forNoKeyUpdate 400. SQLite has no row locks 
arrayContains, arrayOverlaps, jsonContains 400

chunks.h: What works on SQLite, and what is a 400?
chunks.t: Driver errors map to HTTP the same way as on the other dialects: a UNIQUE or primary key violation is a 409 DuplicateEntityException, a FOREIGN KEY violation is a 400 on a write and a 409 on a delete, and NOT NULL or CHECK is a 400 ValidationFailedException. Since 3.7.2 so are the type errors: a STRICT table refusing "abc" for an integer column (extended code 3091) and SQLITE_MISMATCH ("abc" for an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY). SQLite does not report the duplicate value, so the message names the column only.

chunks.h: How many values can one SQLite statement bind?
chunks.t: 32,766 on SQLite and libSQL, the default SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER, and 100 on Cloudflare D1. The service counts the bound parameters of every statement and answers one past the limit with a 400 that names both numbers, instead of the driver's too many SQL variables (a 500). It tells D1 apart by the Drizzle instance you pass. A massCreate of 2,000 rows with 20 columns binds 40,000 values, so split it in two on SQLite. If your SQLite build allows more, override the protected bindLimit(db) method.

chunks.h: How do I use Cloudflare D1?
chunks.t:
Build the instance from the binding with drizzle-orm/d1 and pass it as db, with dialect: 'sqlite'. D1 rejects BEGIN and SAVEPOINT, so everything that needs a transaction throws a TransactionException before it sends a statement:

- massCreate, massUpdate, massUpsert, massSoftDelete, massRestore, massDelete and massForceDelete
- a create with nested relations
- attach, detach and sync

The single-row methods (create, update, upsert, softDelete, restore, delete, every read) do not need one. For several writes that must succeed together on D1, call db.batch([...]) with Drizzle yourself.

What has been tested. 
The package's own suite runs every SQLite feature above against libSQL in memory. The D1 and
synchronous driver refusals are tested against a stand-in object that reports itself the way
those drivers do, not against D1 or better-sqlite3 themselves.

Does nestjs-drizzle-crud support SQLite?. 
Yes, since 3.7.0, with dialect: "sqlite" and a Drizzle instance you pass as db. libSQL (@libsql/client) runs every feature that SQLite has. Full-text search, row locks and the array and JSON operators are a 400.

Can I use better-sqlite3?. 
For the single-row methods and every read, it should: Drizzle makes every better-sqlite3 query awaitable, though the package's suite does not run on it. Mass writes, nested creates and attach / detach / sync throw a TransactionException, because a better-sqlite3 transaction cannot wait for async work. Use libSQL with a file: URL for a local database that supports them.

Why are bulk writes not available on Cloudflare D1?. 
They run in one interactive transaction, and a failure is replayed with a savepoint per item, so a failing item can be named and everything rolled back. D1 has no interactive transactions, only batch(), so the package refuses those calls with a clear error instead of writing half a batch.

Is LIKE case-sensitive on SQLite?. 
No, not for ASCII letters: SQLite's LIKE matches Ann and ann alike. That is why, since 3.7.2, contains, startsWith and endsWith use GLOB when sql.caseSensitive is true, which compares case exactly. The like operator and the i forms stay LIKE.

chunks.h: Test a NestJS Drizzle CRUD service
chunks.t:
Test a NestJS Drizzle CRUD service against real SQL in memory with PGlite, or unit test it with TestCrudFactory and a Jest mock database.

To test a NestJS Drizzle CRUD service, boot it through DrizzleCrudModule against PGlite, an in-memory Postgres, so every filter, soft delete and constraint runs as real SQL with no server or container. For narrow unit tests, the package also exports TestCrudFactory, which builds the service on a Jest mock database that runs no SQL, and BaseCrudSpecHelper, a base class around it.

A mock cannot check your SQL. 
The mock database accepts any query, so it cannot catch a wrong column key, a bad cast or a
constraint violation. The package added its own PGlite suite after mocked tests let real bugs
through. Use the mock for logic in your service, and PGlite for anything that
touches the database.
